title: 'Improving Food Security for the People of Gaza' Independent Evaluation
file_title: Evaluation of the progress of the 'Improving Food Security for the People of Gaza' programme
description: This document describes an evaluation of the effectiveness of DFID-funded programs aimed at improving food security and reducing poverty in Gaza from 2011-2015, including the UNRWA Job Creation Programme and the WFP Voucher Programme. The evaluation methodology encompassed fieldwork, consultations, data analysis, and focus group discussions, despite facing challenges due to Gaza's complex political situation and reliance on external data. The findings reveal that the programs had moderate success in improving food consumption and economic well-being, but were less effective in achieving long-term poverty reduction, with the WFP's voucher program showing more sustainability and effectiveness than UNRWA's job creation efforts. The evaluation suggests that DFID consider alternative support mechanisms and that implementing partners expand voucher platforms and local sourcing. It also highlights the need for improved coordination among agencies, strengthened monitoring and evaluation, and the consideration of the wider political context in funding decisions.

title: A Multi-Donor Evaluation of Support to Conflict Prevention and Peacebuilding Activities in Southern Sudan 2005-2010
file_title: Aiding the peace
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of donor-supported initiatives for conflict prevention, peacebuilding, and development in Southern Sudan from 2005 to 2010. The evaluation examines the impact of international assistance on conflict dynamics, particularly in anticipation of the 2011 independence referendum, and assesses the effectiveness of aid in various sectors including emergency relief, governance, health, education, and agriculture. Methodologically, the evaluation employs tools such as the OECD/DAC criteria, the Utstein Palette, and the Strategic Conflict Assessment, and involves context analysis, conflict mapping, and performance reviews over a five-year period. The findings reveal that despite significant donor contributions, challenges such as poor coordination, inadequate conflict analysis, a development-focused approach, and practical difficulties hindered the effectiveness of interventions. The evaluation highlights the complexity of the aid-conflict relationship and the need for more nuanced, politically informed, and flexible approaches. Recommendations include improving governance, rule of law, security sector reform, community engagement, and ensuring aid aligns with government priorities and conflict-sensitive strategies. The document also underscores the importance of harmonizing aid with the Comprehensive Peacebuilding Programme and the role of non-DAC donors in the region's development.

title: A Synthesis of Population Project Evaluations
file_title: A Synthesis of Population Project Evaluations (ev598)
description: This document describes an evaluation of the transition from the Overseas Development Administration (ODA) to the Department For International Development (DFID) in relation to family planning and reproductive health projects. The evaluation, which incorporates findings from four studies, examines the design, implementation, and sustainability of ODA-funded projects, highlighting design flaws and imprecise indicators. It notes the variable success of NGO-implemented projects and the difficulties in reaching the poorest populations and sustaining programs without ongoing external support. The document stresses the need for clear poverty-focused strategies, effective information and education programs, and donor involvement to ensure access to family planning services. It also discusses the importance of NGO roles, community participation, and reliable performance measures, concluding that continued support and clear procedures are vital for the success and sustainability of these initiatives. The evaluation underscores the necessity of diverse contraceptive methods, education, access to services for marginalized groups, financial sustainability, effective project design, national commitment, and a combination of factors for the success of family planning programs, along with recommendations for enhancing effectiveness.

title: Adaptation Learning Programme (ALP) Care International
file_title: Adaptation Learning Program: Final Evaluation Report
description: This document describes an evaluation of CARE International's Adaptation Learning Programme (ALP), which aims to enhance the capacity of vulnerable households in sub-Saharan Africa to adapt to climate change, with a focus on gender equality and diversity. The evaluation, conducted by the Nottawasaga Institute, used a participatory approach to assess the program's progress in Ghana, Niger, Kenya, and Mozambique. It found that the ALP had effectively engaged communities and facilitated dialogue platforms for climate resilience, though results varied across countries. Challenges were identified in documenting and evaluating community-based adaptation (CBA) models for policy advocacy, and recommendations were made to strengthen the program's framework, improve gender skills, and enhance communication strategies. The evaluation concluded that while the ALP has been robust and has influenced government policies to some extent, it needs more targeted communication, capacity building, and evidence-based advocacy to effectively address climate change.

title: Adolescent Girls Empowerment Programme, Zambia

description: The evaluation of the Girls Empowerment Programme in Zambia assessed its effectiveness in enhancing the social, health, and economic assets of adolescent girls through various interventions, including Safe Spaces, health vouchers, and savings accounts. Employing a mixed-method approach, the evaluation found positive outcomes in areas like condom use and school attendance, particularly among younger rural girls, but results were inconclusive for building social assets. The programme faced challenges in implementation, curriculum relevance, and community support, which varied between urban and rural settings. The evaluation recommended modifications to the theory of change, curriculum customization, and improved community engagement, while noting the high cost per participant and the need for further research on long-term benefits. The report concluded with interim findings, emphasizing the importance of credible comparisons with other programmes and the need for future improvements to address the identified challenges.

title: Assessing Value for Money in DFID's Health Portfolio for Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha, India
file_title: Evaluation of the Value for Money in DFID’s Health Portfolio for Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha, India
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of DFID's health interventions in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, and Odisha, India, assessing their value for money and impact on health systems. The evaluation employed various methodological approaches, including the '4Es' framework, REEEES framework, and Paris Declaration Principles, to analyze the effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability of DFID's financial and technical assistance. Results across the evaluations showed that DFID's support was generally aligned with government strategies and contributed to improvements in health outcomes, particularly in maternal and child health, nutrition, and sanitation. However, evidence of efficiency gains was mixed, and challenges such as data quality, attribution of impact, and sustainability post-financial aid were noted. Recommendations included improving value for money measurements, targeting technical assistance, and ensuring sustainable health system developments. The evaluations concluded that while DFID's interventions have potential for long-term benefits, there is a need for continued focus on equity, sustainability, and better coordination among development partners.

title: Baseline Technical Report prepared by Edoren on behalf of UNICEF GEP3
file_title: Technical report
description: This document summarizes the evaluation of the Girls Education Project Phase 3 (GEP3) in Nigeria by the Education Data, Research and Evaluation in Nigeria (EDOREN) consortium. GEP3 is designed to improve school access, retention, and learning outcomes for girls in northern Nigeria, with a focus on early learning interventions and support to Integrated Qur’anic Schools. The evaluation used a theory-based approach, including a clustered randomized controlled trial, and employed various methodologies such as interviews, fieldwork, and data analysis. Key findings reveal operational challenges, the need for improved teacher quality, gender-sensitive teaching, and Hausa language proficiency. Concerns were raised about government funding, teacher motivation, and gender biases. title: CLEAR Midterm Evaluation
file_title: The Centres for Learning on Evaluation and Results (CLEAR): midterm evaluation
description: The CLEAR Midterm Evaluation report examines the CLEAR initiative, which was established in 2010 with the goal of enhancing monitoring and evaluation (M&E) capacity in developing countries. The initiative is supported by multiple partners and managed by the World Bank. The evaluation, conducted by ePact and Universalia Management Group Ltd., utilized interviews, site visits, and document reviews to assess CLEAR's progress, challenges, and impact between 2010 and 2013. It found that CLEAR's relevance to global aid effectiveness discussions is clear, but it lacks specific success definitions and mechanisms for testing its assumptions. The CLEAR Secretariat has been effective in administration, but the Board needs more diversity and strategic guidance. Regional centers have made uneven progress and require clearer strategies and success measures. The evaluation recommends establishing Regional Advisory Committees, developing center-specific theories of change, and reformulating the global learning component. It also suggests the need for strategic partnerships, improved learning opportunities, and regional capacity development. The report concludes with recommendations for the overall program, regional components, and the global learning component, highlighting the need for clearer strategies, theories of change, and data collection to assess long-term effects. It also notes the lack of evidence of positive changes from interventions and the need for more explicit consideration of the enabling environment.

description: This document describes an overview of the ColaLife Operational Trial Zambia (COTZ), which aimed to enhance the accessibility and use of Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) and zinc for treating diarrhea in children under five by utilizing Coca-Cola's distribution channels. The evaluation, conducted by Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, employed a pre-test/post-test design with control groups and gathered data through surveys of caregivers and private retailers. The findings revealed a notable increase in ORS and zinc usage, improved ORS preparation at home, a shift in ORS sourcing from public to private retailers, and heightened awareness of zinc as a treatment. Despite logistical and potential bias challenges, the trial was successful in making essential diarrhea treatments more available, indicating a sustainable positive impact on community health.

title: Country Programme Evaluation Afghanistan
file_title: Country programme evaluation - Afghanistan (EV 696)
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Department for International Development's (DFID) country programme in Afghanistan from 2002 to 2007, with updates for 2008. The evaluation, led by Jon Bennett and his team, aimed to assess the effectiveness of DFID's efforts in providing humanitarian assistance, supporting transitional plans, and contributing to Afghanistan's interim development strategy. The methodological approach included collaboration with DFID country office staff and independent international consultants. The findings revealed progress in health and education but persistent challenges with opium production, unemployment, and corruption. The evaluation highlighted DFID's quick aid disbursement and support for the National Solidarity Programme, while also pointing out issues such as corruption and limited public administration reform. Recommendations for DFID focused on prioritizing rule of law, justice, engagement with Afghan civil society, and addressing gender and human rights issues. The report emphasized the complexity of the Afghan context and the necessity for a sustained international commitment to development and governance. DFID Afghanistan has incorporated these recommendations into its new country plan, and the evaluation department intends to monitor the implementation of these suggestions.

title: Country Programme Evaluation: Ethiopia
file_title: Country programme evaluation: Ethiopia (EV697)
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of DFID's Country Programme in Ethiopia from 2003 to 2008, examining its strategy, interventions, and development programs. The evaluation, conducted by independent consultants and through internal reviews, focused on the effectiveness, efficiency, impact, and sustainability of the programs, which aimed to reduce poverty, improve governance, and enhance basic service delivery in sectors like education, health, and water. Despite challenges in democratic governance, civil society engagement, and regional disparities, DFID's aid was found to be largely aligned with the Ethiopian government's poverty reduction strategies and pro-poor agendas. title: Cross Programme Gender Evaluation
file_title: Cross Programme Gender Evaluation
description: This document describes an evaluation of various programs under the DFID-Z portfolio in Zambia, all aimed at promoting gender equality and the empowerment of women and girls. The programs target a range of issues, including economic empowerment, violence prevention, health, education, and legislative reform, with the overarching goal of achieving gender equality in line with the Gender Strategy's Theory of Change. The evaluation methods included portfolio mapping, program document reviews, interviews, and the use of specific indicators. Results show that while there is engagement in several areas, critical aspects such as women's leadership, economic empowerment, and support for civil society advocacy are lacking. The evaluations conclude that DFID-Z is not fully on track to meet its gender vision by 2015 and recommend refining the portfolio, ensuring full ownership of the Gender Strategy within the DFID-Z office, and better positioning within Zambia's change environment. Additionally, the evaluations highlight the need for challenging social norms, engaging traditional leaders, and focusing on collective empowerment beyond financial assets. Recommendations also emphasize the importance of a balanced approach to gender advisory support, improved coordination with partners, and prioritizing areas with the most impact on gender equality and women's empowerment.

title: DFID Global Social Exclusion Stocktake Report
file_title: DFID Global social exclusion stocktake report (Ev707)
description: This document describes an evaluation of the effectiveness of the Department for International Development's (DFID) Social Exclusion Policy, which aims to combat global social exclusion and enhance poverty reduction efforts. The evaluation, conducted in February 2010 by Julia Betts, Sadie Watson, and Cathy Gaynor, employed a mixed-method approach, including document review, interviews, and analysis of resources and partnerships. It found that awareness and implementation of the policy within DFID were low, despite some progress in integrating social exclusion considerations into areas such as conflict and growth. The evaluation highlighted the need for better corporate systems and incentives to focus on exclusion and improved tracking of resources allocated to this issue. It concluded that DFID's response to social exclusion is fragmented and lacks a strategic approach, recommending a clearer internal position on exclusion, integration of its political aspects, and joint evaluations with development partners. Additionally, the document assesses DFID's integration of social exclusion indicators into its country programs, particularly through the use of Gender and Social Exclusion Analysis (GSEA). The evaluation, which included country case studies and reviews of policy commitment, found an increasing demand for exclusion-focused studies but identified a lack of a common framework for addressing exclusion and insufficient consideration of exclusion in funding to multilateral agencies. While there are examples of good practice in countries like India and Ethiopia, the evaluation recommends making GSEA mandatory for country planning, developing a clear stance on exclusion, and improving collaboration with civil society and multilateral partners. DFID faces a decision to either scale up its activities focused on exclusion or consider alternative strategies, with the possibility of relaunching or refreshing the policy to ensure better accountability and effectiveness.

title: DFID Global Social Exclusion Stocktake Report AES

description: This document serves as an annex to an evaluation report on the Department for International Development's (DFID) efforts to combat global social exclusion, with a focus on Ethiopia and India. The evaluation, conducted in February 2010, assesses DFID's progress since a 2005 policy paper on reducing poverty through addressing social exclusion. Various methods, including desk reviews, interviews, and case studies, were used to evaluate DFID's recognition of social exclusion's role in poverty reduction and the challenges in measuring and implementing effective policies. The report calls for a strategic approach to tackle social exclusion, improved governance to promote social agendas, and better tracking of resources dedicated to these issues. In Ethiopia, DFID's contributions to social change were evaluated, revealing the need for better data on excluded groups, integration of inclusive principles into strategies, and a systematic approach to address exclusion. Recommendations for DFID-E include mainstreaming gender and social exclusion in programs, enhancing statistical capacity, and engaging in policy dialogue. The evaluation of DFID's work in India highlighted progress in incorporating social exclusion analysis into program design, especially concerning gender and caste. However, improvements are needed in addressing other dimensions such as religion, disability, and HIV status. The evaluation suggests that DFID's corporate structure supports the social exclusion agenda but requires more consistent application and monitoring. Recommendations include enhancing civil society dialogue, strengthening partnerships, and building DFID's capacity to tackle structural barriers to social exclusion. The evaluation also identifies growth and climate change as new policy areas for integrating social exclusion considerations.

title: DFID Sudan. Darfur Community Peace and Stability Fund Impact Assessment

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Darfur Community Peace and Stability Fund (DCPSF), which is designed to foster peace and stability in Darfur by encouraging community conflict resolution and grassroots initiatives, with a particular emphasis on involving women and youth. The evaluation, carried out in December 2012, employed qualitative methods due to the absence of centralized data and built upon a 2010 review. The results showed significant achievements in community cooperation and conflict resolution, though some areas saw little progress. Success factors, obstacles, and suggestions for future enhancement were identified. Despite facing security and sustainability challenges, the DCPSF has positively influenced peace and stability in Darfur, especially by increasing women's participation in peace processes and youth in leadership. The evaluation underscores the necessity for more research on participant perspectives, improved monitoring, and overcoming socio-cultural barriers to women's involvement.

title: Delivering Reproductive Health Results (DRHR) through Non-State Providers in Pakistan

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Delivering Reproductive Health Results (DRHR) program in Pakistan, which is designed to enhance access to reproductive health services via non-state providers. The program's goals include increasing knowledge and use of modern contraceptive methods, particularly among poorer households, and improving the overall quality of reproductive health services. The evaluation utilized a range of methodological approaches, including primary data collection, Propensity Score Matching, and differences in differences analysis. Results showed positive impacts on awareness and service quality, with a modest targeting towards poorer households, but the program did not significantly change overall access and utilization of contraceptives. The evaluation also noted methodological limitations and suggested the need for further analysis and program adjustments. It concluded that while non-state providers are important in service delivery, the program's effectiveness in overcoming major barriers to reproductive health remains uncertain, and future evaluations should incorporate qualitative data for a more complete understanding.

title: Evaluating Tanzania's Productive Social Safety Net
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of Tanzania's Productive Social Safety Net (PSSN) program, which is designed to reduce poverty and improve various socioeconomic outcomes for its beneficiaries. The program's effectiveness was assessed through randomized control trials and various statistical analyses using data from the 2017 PSSN Midline Impact Evaluation. The findings reveal that the PSSN has had a positive impact on household consumption, food security, education enrollment, health service utilization, labor dynamics, housing conditions, and asset ownership. It has also led to a decrease in unemployment rates, with a more pronounced effect on males, and has shifted non-farm enterprises towards more profitable sectors. While the program has increased women's decision-making power and reduced child labor, it has not significantly affected traditional labor outcomes or agricultural asset ownership. Despite its successes, the program has not fully alleviated poverty, indicating a need for sustained support and improvements. The evaluation suggests the potential for a National Social Registry and emphasizes the importance of long-term commitment and coordination for significant poverty reduction.

As Twaweza transitions to new leadership, the evaluation suggests strategic revisions and continued donor support to enhance its effectiveness.

description: This document describes an evaluation of the DFID Somalia 2013-2017 Humanitarian Programme, which was designed to deliver humanitarian aid, enhance resilience, and reform the humanitarian system in Somalia. The findings reveal that the programme is ambitious and relevant, with its multi-year funding and partnerships fostering improved delivery and innovation. However, there are challenges in demonstrating effectiveness, coherence in definitions and approaches, and issues with gender equality and climate change strategies. The evaluation also highlights the need for standardized definitions and tools across partner activities, better coordination, and operationalizing risk strategies. Despite these innovations, there are difficulties with excessive information requests, misalignment between humanitarian and development efforts, and challenges in data sharing and technology implementation. Recommendations include refining the Theory of Change, developing common definitions, improving partner collaboration, and enhancing the M&E system to address these challenges and improve the programme's impact.

title: Evaluation of Results Based Aid in Rwandan Education

description: This document summarizes evaluations of the Results-Based Aid (RBA) program in Rwandan education, which aimed to enhance educational outcomes, particularly student completion rates and English language proficiency among teachers. Various methodologies, including econometric modeling, qualitative research, and value for money analysis, were employed to assess the program's effectiveness. Findings across the evaluations suggest that while there were improvements in educational outcomes, RBA was not the sole or primary factor influencing these changes. Increases in completion rates were often attributed to other policy changes and existing government and community efforts. The program's impact on English proficiency showed mixed results with data comparability issues. Recommendations include refining performance measures and considering the political context in future RBA applications. The evaluations also emphasize the importance of context in assessing interventions and suggest a realist approach for future studies. Limitations such as data quality and political sensitivities were noted, and stakeholder engagement was highlighted as crucial for the evaluation process.

title: Evaluation of Silvicultural Research Project and Forestry Research Project in Nepal
file_title: Evaluation Of Silvicultural Research Project And Forestry Research Project I, Nepal (ev529)
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Silvicultural Research Project (SRP) and Forestry Research Project (FRP) in Nepal, funded by the UK's ODA from 1979-1990, which aimed to enhance forestry research capabilities. The evaluation employed desk studies, field missions, and surveys, identifying that the projects successfully established a research facility and produced publications but struggled with institutional development, sustainability, and dissemination of findings. Key issues included a lack of research priority analysis, absence of socio-economic research, and limited end-user involvement. The projects were found to be cost-effective and had institutional impacts, but improvements were needed in research planning and coordination. The evaluation also assessed the Nepal-UK Silvicultural and Forestry Research Project's dissemination and impact on forestry practices, revealing that higher-level professionals were more informed than technicians. Recommendations for future projects include clear dissemination strategies, better research-extension coordination, and a multi-media approach to reach broader audiences. Historical milestones such as the creation of the Forestry Research and Information Centre and the Forestry Sector Master Plan were also noted.

title: Evaluation of Water & Sanitation for the Urban Poor's DFID-funded Programme 2012-2015

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Water & Sanitation for the Urban Poor (WSUP) program, which seeks to enhance water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services for low-income urban populations. The program's strategies include infrastructure development, community engagement, cost recovery through user fees, and efficiency improvements. Evaluations were conducted using a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods, such as interviews, surveys, and independent verification across multiple countries. Results show that WSUP exceeded its service provision targets, positively impacting millions of direct and indirect beneficiaries, and demonstrated cost-effectiveness. The program has also been influential in changing local utilities' approaches to pro-poor services and has become a knowledge leader in the sector. Despite these successes, challenges remain in ensuring long-term sustainability and addressing the needs of the poorest consumers. Recommendations for WSUP include continued institutional support, refining monitoring systems, advocating for sector-wide changes, and enhancing research and training to further influence WASH policies and practices.

title: Evaluation of the Conflict Prevention Pools: Sierra Leone
file_title: Evaluation of the Conflict Prevention Pools: Sierra Leone
description: This document describes an evaluation of the UK's Conflict Prevention Pools (CPPs), particularly the Africa Conflict Prevention Pool (ACPP), and their role in Sierra Leone. The CPPs, established in 2001, aim to prevent and reduce violent conflict through a collaborative approach involving multiple UK government departments. The evaluation, led by Jeremy Ginifer, employed a case study methodology in Sierra Leone, revealing that while the CPPs support important conflict prevention activities, there are areas for improvement in coordination, response, and resource allocation. The UK's efforts in Sierra Leone have contributed to peace maintenance and conflict prevention, with notable achievements in security sector reform and ex-combatant reintegration. However, addressing the underlying causes of conflict, such as poverty and corruption, remains a challenge. Recommendations include setting more realistic benchmarks, enhancing local ownership, and improving coordination. The document also reviews the UK Strategy for Conflict Prevention in Sierra Leone, highlighting the need for continued engagement and improved targets, especially in light of the UNAMSIL withdrawal. It suggests local leadership, NGO engagement, security sector reform, and shared financial responsibilities with international partners as key strategies. The document acknowledges contributors and provides additional resources and contact information for DFID.

title: Evaluation of the DFID/WHO partnership
file_title: Evaluation of the DFID /WHO Partnership: Synthesis report
description: This document describes an evaluation of the partnership between the UK Department for International Development (DFID) and the World Health Organization (WHO), assessing its alignment with health-related Millennium Development Goals and poverty reduction efforts. The evaluation, led by Phil Compernolle and Catherine Cameron, employed qualitative methods and stakeholder feedback due to the limited sample size. It found that while the partnership is valued and goals are shared, there are significant challenges in communication, trust, and implementing shared objectives, particularly at the country level. DFID's shift to un-earmarked funding for WHO reflects trust but raises concerns about WHO's performance and the effectiveness of its monitoring and evaluation. The evaluation suggests that the partnership has potential but requires clearer role definitions, improved trust, and a focus on pro-poor technical programs that address inequalities. It also discusses DFID's funding strategies, the importance of regular meetings and technical dialogue, the role of regional WHO offices, and the impact of secondments. The evaluation methodology included thematic analysis, stakeholder questioning, and country case studies to assess the partnership's value beyond a mere contractual relationship.

title: Evaluation of the Developing Operational Research Capacity in the Health Sector Project
file_title: Evaluation of the Developing Operational Research Capacity in the Health Sector Project
description: The Developing Operational Research Capacity in the Health Sector Project, funded by DFID and the Bloomberg Foundation and implemented by The Union, was evaluated for its effectiveness in enhancing operational research (OR) skills among health sector professionals to improve health service delivery in developing countries. The project focused on diseases such as HIV/AIDS, TB, and Malaria and included training and mentoring components. Evaluation methods encompassed interviews, questionnaires, case studies, bibliometric analysis, and participant surveys. Results showed that the project significantly improved OR knowledge and skills, led to a high number of scientific publications, and had a positive impact on health systems and policies. Gender balance was achieved among participants, and the project was found to be cost-efficient with potential for regional expansion. Recommendations for future improvements include a more transparent selection process, involvement of health ministries, and the establishment of formal alumni networks. The evaluation suggests that the training model could be expanded to other health research areas and highlights the importance of sustainable local OR networks.

description: This document describes an evaluation of the Future Agricultures Consortium (FAC), which aims to influence agricultural policy and build research capacity in Africa. The evaluation, conducted by Upper Quartile using a RAPID Outcome Assessment approach and various other methods, finds that FAC's activities are relevant and have contributed to policy design and advocacy, with notable impacts in countries like Kenya, Malawi, and Ethiopia. However, it identifies gaps in gender mainstreaming, engagement processes, and systematic monitoring. Recommendations include improving monitoring systems, management capacity, African leadership, sustainable funding, and communication strategies. file_title: Evaluation of the Growth in Rural Economy and Agriculture in Tajikistan (GREAT)
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Growth in the Rural Economy and Agriculture Tajikistan (GREAT) program, which aimed to stimulate economic growth in rural Tajikistan, particularly through agricultural development and improved access to financial products. The program focused on creating a conducive business environment, enhancing market linkages, and promoting gender equity and poverty reduction. Various evaluation methods, including interviews, surveys, and data analysis, were used to assess the program's relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, and sustainability. The findings revealed that the program was relevant and had some positive impacts, such as establishing business associations and improving the business environment. However, challenges were identified in achieving national level changes, ensuring sustainability, and integrating gender considerations. The program was effective in supporting agricultural activities, with the Sarob model being particularly successful, but faced issues with under-mechanization and the effectiveness of monitoring frameworks. In the non-agriculture sector, the program supported energy-efficient enterprises, but sustainability and scalability were concerns. The program's financial interventions were crucial for private sector growth, though broader reach and stronger policy connections were needed. Overall, the evaluations indicated that while the program had positive outcomes, there were limitations that needed to be addressed in future initiatives.

title: Evaluation of the Ghana Electoral Support Programme
file_title: Evaluation of the Ghana Electoral Support Programme
description: The Ghana Electoral Support Programme (GESP) was evaluated to determine its effectiveness in promoting free, fair, and peaceful elections in Ghana. The program focused on capacity building and training for key stakeholders, including the Electoral Commission, judiciary, security forces, and civil society organizations. Various methods such as document reviews, interviews, and surveys were used in the evaluation. The GESP was found to be largely successful in addressing electoral challenges, improving election support capacity, and contributing to credible elections. However, issues such as technical difficulties with Biometric Voter Registration, the need for better coordination, and sustainability were identified. Recommendations for future programs include long-term engagement, realistic timeframes, strategic partnerships, and a focus on social inclusion. The program was completed mostly on time and within budget, offering good value for money with evidence of sustainable outcomes, but highlighted areas for improvement in risk management and gender-social inclusion. Overall, the GESP had a positive impact on the 2012 elections in Ghana, with suggestions for extending support throughout the entire election cycle.

title: Evaluation of the Somalia Stability Programme
file_title: Evaluation of the Somalia Stability programme
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Somalia Stability Programme Pilots, which aim to support community-driven development, peace-building, and stability in Somalia, particularly in light of recent political changes and the diminishing influence of Al Shabaab. The evaluation used interviews, document reviews, and field visits to assess the delivery of results, theories of change, project resilience, and adherence to Do No Harm principles. Results indicate that while there is good risk mitigation in pilot programs, there is a need for improved outcomes, impact measurement, and clarity in theories of change. Recommendations include independent evaluations, developing tailored theories of change, integrating the British Office for Somalia (BOFS) Stabilisation Team into programming, re-branding the Stability Support Programme (SSP), and focusing on South Central Somalia. The evaluation also highlights the importance of financial accountability, cultural sensitivity, and the role of clans and diaspora as both barriers and enablers. It suggests that stability programming should be more geographically and thematically focused, with clear definitions of success and consistent organizational resilience. The document concludes with a call for better monitoring and evaluation, including the development of qualitative indicators and a learning component within the SSP.

The main conclusions indicate that the Declaration is often seen as donor-driven, with a need for political re-engagement, better incentive systems, and stronger mutual accountability mechanisms. Recommendations for improving aid effectiveness include continued high-level political engagement, involvement of a wider range of stakeholders, and strengthening partner country systems, while adapting the approach to different country contexts and providing clear policy guidance. description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the UK's development cooperation with Vietnam, with a focus on the Department for International Development's (DFID) efforts towards sustainable poverty reduction, Millennium Development Goals, wealth creation, and governance improvements. Employing a mixed-methods approach, including Adaptive Theory, interviews, field visits, and case studies, the evaluation assesses the effectiveness, efficiency, and impact of the UK's aid, which amounted to £481 million since 1998. Results show that DFID's assistance has contributed to poverty reduction, but with mixed success in reaching the poorest and ethnic minorities. The evaluation highlights the need for improved governance, donor coordination, and local government engagement. It also addresses the challenges of DFID's exit strategy from bilateral cooperation with Vietnam. The findings aim to inform future development efforts and provide lessons learned, while acknowledging the uncertainties in Vietnam's path to further poverty reduction.

title: Evaluation of the pilot project of Results-Based Aid in the education sector in Ethiopia
file_title: Evaluation: Pilot Project of Results-Based Aid in the Education Sector, Ethiopia
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Results-Based Aid (RBA) pilot project in Ethiopia's education sector from 2004-2006, which aimed to enhance lower secondary education by linking aid to performance outcomes. The evaluation, conducted by Cambridge Education and Mott MacDonald, employed a mixed-method approach, including econometric modeling and interviews. It assessed the impact on exam pass rates, gender and regional equity, institutional consequences, and value for money. The findings revealed that the RBA pilot did not significantly improve educational outcomes or equity, and encountered challenges such as communication issues and delayed payments. Despite the lack of significant impact, the pilot provided insights for future RBA initiatives. The evaluation recommended setting realistic expectations, engaging local stakeholders, and designing structured evaluations for future RBA programs.

title: Evaluation of the social and economic impacts of Tuungane
file_title: Evaluation of the social and economic impacts of Tuungane
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Tuungane project, a community-driven initiative in the Democratic Republic of Congo aimed at fostering social cohesion, improving local governance, and stimulating economic recovery. The project focused on leadership training, governance, and the construction of community infrastructure. A randomized intervention method and various data collection tools were used to assess the program's impact on social, economic, and behavioral outcomes. The evaluation revealed that despite successful project implementation, there were minimal improvements in social cohesion, economic status, or behavioral changes. The inclusion of women in committees and the gender parity requirement showed only weak positive effects on trust and no significant economic benefits. The results suggest that the Community-Driven Development model may not be as effective in achieving desired outcomes as proponents suggest, with limited and varied effects on governance and social cohesion. The evaluation also discusses challenges such as potential biases, noncompliance, spillover effects, and data loss due to political and logistical issues. Overall, the Tuungane project had some positive effects but was largely ineffective in several key areas, indicating a need for further research and program design improvement.

title: Evaluation of: The Caribbean Aid for Trade and Regional Integration Trust Fund (CARTFund)
file_title: Evaluation of: The Caribbean Aid for Trade and Regional Integration Trust Fund (CARTFUND)
description: The evaluation report by International Financial Consulting Ltd. reviews the Caribbean Aid for Trade and Regional Integration Trust Fund (CARTFund), which was established to enhance Caribbean trade with Europe and promote regional integration. The fund aimed to support the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) and the Caribbean Single Market and Economy (CSME), focusing on areas such as the health and wellness industry, tourism, and export readiness. The evaluation employed a variety of research methods, including field missions and interviews, to assess the fund's design, strategy, and effectiveness. Results showed that while CARTFund had positive impacts, such as capacity building and increased awareness of trade agreements, it faced challenges in project implementation, strategic focus, and gender inclusiveness. Private sector projects outperformed public sector ones, but issues with unrealistic targets and stakeholder engagement were noted. The report recommended improvements in project management, capacity building, and a more strategic approach to resource allocation. It also emphasized the need for continued donor support and highlighted 18 key recommendations to enhance the effectiveness of future trade-related initiatives in the Caribbean.

title: External Evaluation Report of Sierra Leone's Youth Reproductive Health Programme (2007 - 2012)
file_title: Management response to the evaluation of Sierra Leone’s Youth Reproductive Health Programme 2007–2012
description: This document describes an evaluation of the Youth Empowerment Program (YEP) and the Youth Leadership and Advocacy Program (YLAP) implemented by Restless Development in Sierra Leone, which aimed to improve sexual and reproductive health, civic participation, and livelihoods among young people. Funded by DFID, the program employed peer-to-peer strategies and capacity building to effect behavioral change. A quasi-experimental study design was used for evaluation, showing positive outcomes in sexual health behaviors and increased access to health services. The program was noted for its efficiency, sustainability, and replicability, overcoming challenges such as cultural barriers and resource limitations. It achieved significant improvements in areas like condom use, STI treatment, and HIV/AIDS knowledge, and successfully engaged in advocacy for the inclusion of sexual and reproductive health in school curricula. The evaluation, based on both quantitative and qualitative data, concluded that the program was effective and aligned with national policies, but recommended a revised sustainability strategy and a continued focus on comprehensive HIV prevention.

title: External evaluation of the Southern African Regional Social and Behaviour Change Communication Programme
file_title: DFID Management response to the external evaluation of the Southern Africa Regional Social and Behaviour Change Communic
description: This document describes an evaluation of the effectiveness of various media programs in influencing HIV-related behaviors and attitudes across different African countries. Programs like OneLove radio, SAfAIDS, and Community Media Trust aimed to increase HIV awareness, discussions, and behavior change. The evaluation used a post-only, cross-sectional design with structured interviews and statistical analyses to compare outcomes between individuals exposed to the interventions and those who were not. Results indicated that these programs were generally cost-effective, with radio and television being the most cost-effective channels. The OneLove campaign, in particular, was successful in increasing risk perception, altering social norms, and encouraging behavior change to decrease HIV transmission. The evaluation found that while these interventions had a significant impact on HIV knowledge and attitudes, their effects on actual risk behaviors were more limited. However, there were notable improvements in community responses to HIV, such as increased testing and condom use, especially among high-risk populations. The evaluation concluded that sustained mass media efforts and localized strategies can be highly effective in the fight against HIV/AIDS, with radio and print media showing the strongest evidence of influencing behavior change.

description: This document summarizes the evaluations of the Palestinian Facility for New Market Development (FNMD), a program designed to bolster Palestinian SMEs by providing grants for market and product development. The FNMD, implemented by DAI Europe and funded by DFID and the World Bank, was assessed for its relevance, effectiveness, impact, and sustainability using OECD-DAC criteria. The evaluations found that the program aligned with local and DFID strategies, exceeded its targets, and had a positive national impact, including job creation and market penetration. Despite data collection challenges, the FNMD was praised for its practical results and business-led approach. title: Final Baseline Technical Report, Volume I: Results and Discussion
file_title: Teacher Development Programme: Baseline Technical Report Volume 1
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Teacher Development Programme's (TDP) In-Service Teacher Training in northern Nigeria, aimed at enhancing teaching quality and student learning outcomes. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the evaluation gathered data from primary schools and stakeholders, revealing challenges such as poor student literacy and numeracy, insufficient teacher subject knowledge, and inadequate infrastructure. Key findings include Grade 3 pupils lagging in core subjects, with disparities based on gender and wealth, and teachers needing better training and pedagogical skills. The evaluation also highlights issues such as short lesson times, varied teacher absenteeism, and the critical role of head teachers in school management, despite their limited formal authority. Additionally, it points out the need for better resource allocation, motivation, and training for teachers and head teachers to improve the program's effectiveness. The document suggests that future adjustments to the TDP and ongoing evaluations are necessary to ensure its success.

title: Final Evaluation of the Building Capacity to Use Research Evidence (BCURE) Programme
file_title: Building Capacity to Use Research Evidence (BCURE)
description: The BCURE Evaluation Final Comparative Report by Itad, published in January 2018, critically examines the Building Capacity to Use Research Evidence (BCURE) program, which was designed to improve evidence-informed policymaking in various low and middle-income countries. The evaluation employed a realist approach and diverse methodologies, including qualitative interviews, synthesis reports, and monitoring data, to assess the program's effectiveness in Africa and Asia. Findings revealed that while there were some improvements in skills and knowledge among policymakers, and instances of success in specific sectors, the overall long-term impact of the program remains uncertain. Key factors for the success of evidence-informed policymaking initiatives included political support, strategic engagement, and the creation of organizational platforms. The report also highlighted the importance of flexible, adaptive approaches and the potential for sustained change when interventions are effectively integrated at different levels. However, challenges such as political constraints, capacity limitations, and the need for ongoing government ownership were noted. The evaluation suggests that future efforts should incorporate a Political Economy Analysis to better capture outcome-level changes and address the complexities of promoting routine evidence use in government settings.

title: Final Impact Assessment of the Results-Based Financing Programme for Northern Uganda
file_title: Evaluation of Results Based Financing Programme for Northern Uganda
description: This document summarizes independent evaluations of Results-Based Financing (RBF) health programs in the Acholi and Lango sub-regions of Uganda, conducted by Liverpool Consulting from 2012-2015. The RBF programs aimed to enhance health service access, quality, and affordability, particularly for sick children and pregnant women, with a focus on sustainability. Methodologies included Lot Quality Assurance Sampling (LQAS), Rapid Health Facility Assessment (R-HFA), community surveys, and data analysis. Results showed improvements in service access, essential medicine availability, and reduced user fees, but concerns about the sustainability and quality of clinical care were noted. The RBF programs led to increased health service utilization and improved affordability, but did not adequately address clinical care quality, with persistent deficiencies in diagnosis and counseling. Recommendations from the evaluations suggest prioritizing clinical care quality, integrating quality into RBF payment formulas, and addressing human resource gaps. The evaluations also highlight the need for better alignment of incentive structures with health outcomes and the development of strategies for institutionalizing gains to ensure long-term sustainability.

description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Climate and Development Knowledge Network (CDKN), focusing on its efforts to facilitate climate-resilient development in developing countries. title: Impact Evaluation of DFID's Electoral Programmes in Pakistan
file_title: Impact Evaluation of DFIDs Electoral Programmes in Pakistan
description: This document describes an evaluation of DFID Pakistan's electoral reform and transparency programs, SERP and STAEP, assessing their impact on voter turnout and democratic processes. The evaluation, conducted by the Collective for Social Science Research using Contribution Analysis, combined quantitative and qualitative methods. It found a 17% increase in voter turnout between 2008 and 2013, though the target was not fully met. The programs were seen to have a modest impact on democratic outcomes, with STAEP's election observation noted for creating a sense of scrutiny despite limited scale impact. The evaluation underscores the need to address political behavior, organizational constraints, and social exclusion in future programming and to integrate data requirements into program design. It also recommends maintaining technical assistance 'firefighting' windows in election support programs. The document includes annexes with additional details and acknowledges the contributions of various researchers.

title: Impact Evaluation of the DFID Programme to Accelerate Improved Nutrition for the Extreme Poor in Bangladesh: Final Report
file_title: Evaluation of the DFID programme to accelerate improved nutrition for the extreme poor in Bangladesh
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of various livelihood and nutrition interventions in Bangladesh, funded by DFID and implemented by organizations such as PATH and Concern Worldwide. The interventions aimed to improve nutrition outcomes, particularly for young children, pregnant and lactating mothers, and adolescent girls, by integrating nutrition-specific programs with livelihood support. A mixed-method approach, including household surveys, endline surveys, and qualitative studies, was used to assess the impact on nutritional status, dietary practices, child anthropometry, women's health indicators, and decision-making within households. The evaluations revealed limited improvements in Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) practices, child anthropometry, and women's health indicators. Challenges included the ratio of community nutrition workers to households, training intensity, program duration, and the translation of increased nutrition knowledge into practice. Some positive impacts were observed, such as improved knowledge of iron supplementation and increased consumption of iron-rich foods, but these did not translate into significant changes in dietary diversity, meal frequency, or women's BMI. The interventions also had limited effects on women's decision-making and mobility, although there were some improvements in antenatal care and economic well-being. Recommendations for future programs include increasing the intensity and adaptability of nutrition worker practice, community mobilization, empowering mothers, and prioritizing child diet. The evaluations suggest that while interventions were widely implemented, their impact on beneficiaries' lives varied, and there is a need for more effective coordination between livelihood and nutrition interventions to achieve better outcomes.

The evaluations employed a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods to assess the social and economic impacts of the program. Findings indicated that CLP-1 positively affected household incomes, reduced vulnerability, and improved food security, with some methodological challenges in measuring these impacts. The program also facilitated increased income in sectors not directly supported by CLP-1, improved access to credit, health, nutrition, and social capital. However, sustainability of benefits and systemic changes in market and government systems were limited. The evaluations provided recommendations for future programs, emphasizing the need for clear targets, balanced monitoring, specific participant selection, and improved methodologies. The results and lessons learned will guide the next phase of the program (CLP-2) and contribute to the global evidence base on social protection and support for the extreme poor.

title: Independent Report Midterm Evaluation of Livelihood Enhancement Through Agriculture Development (LEAD) Programme
file_title: Mid Term Evaluation of Livelihood Enhancement through Agriculture Development (LEAD) Programme
description: The mid-term evaluation of the Livelihood Enhancement through Agricultural Development (LEAD) program in Tanzania focused on its effectiveness in enhancing the livelihoods of smallholder maize and poultry farmers. The program's objectives were to improve market access, input availability, and agrifinance, using a Making Markets Work for the Poor (M4P) approach. A mixed-methods evaluation, including household surveys, interviews, and focus groups, was conducted by the e-Pact consortium. Results showed positive impacts on yields and incomes, especially in the poultry sector, with farmers benefiting from market linkages and improved farming practices. However, issues with loan repayments, market access for maize, sustainability, governance, and gender and poverty integration were identified. Recommendations included developing sustainability plans, adapting the agrifinance model, and enhancing data use and reporting. The evaluation called for clearer long-term market change strategies and emphasized the importance of sustainability and scalability in market interventions.

title: Independent Verification and Evaluation of the End Child Marriage Programme: Ethiopia
file_title: End Child Marraige Programme: Ethiopia - midterm report
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the End Child Marriage Programme (ECMP) in Ethiopia, which is designed to delay the age of first marriage for adolescent girls and to end child marriage and female genital mutilation. The evaluation utilized mixed methods, including policy analysis, participatory approaches, interviews, and statistical analysis, to assess the program's progress, impact, and challenges. It found that the ECMP has increased government commitment, trained community facilitators, supported school clubs, and provided economic incentives to households. The program has also involved religious leaders and used media to spread its message. Despite these successes, there are challenges in reaching out-of-school girls, managing economic incentives, and ensuring sustainability due to limited government ownership at regional levels. The evaluation suggests improvements such as refining the program's Theory of Change, developing an exit strategy, and enhancing monitoring and evaluation. It also highlights the need for effective qualitative research and a better understanding of social norm change. The program is considered cost-effective, with health benefits being the most significant, but recommendations include adopting a more affordable model for long-term success. Overall, while the ECMP has made significant strides in bringing child marriage into the open, further efforts are needed to institutionalize the approach within the government and to build a solid evidence base for its effectiveness.

These programs, including the End Child Marriage Programme (ECMP), were launched with the goals of delaying marriage for girls, promoting gender equality, and changing social norms. The evaluations employed qualitative methods, economic analysis, and participatory approaches, involving young evaluators and community stakeholders. title: Independent evaluation of Artemisinin monotherapy replacement in the private sector to support the containment of Artemisinin-resistant malaria in Burma
file_title: Management Response: Myanmar Artemisinin Monotherapy Replacement Malaria Project
description: This document describes a summary of evaluations for the Myanmar Artemisinin Monotherapy Replacement Malaria Project (AMTR), which aimed to combat artemisinin-resistant malaria by promoting the use of quality-assured artemisinin combination therapy (QA-ACT) in the private sector. Funded by UKAid from DFID and supported by partners including the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the project employed a mix of qualitative and quantitative methods to assess its effectiveness. The evaluations revealed that the project successfully increased QA-ACT usage and improved fever treatment, but faced sustainability issues, low testing rates, and difficulties in treating confirmed positive cases. Despite challenges such as illegal imports of monotherapies and risks of expired drugs, the project influenced the market for anti-malarials and raised awareness for malaria testing. Recommendations for future interventions include continued private sector engagement and donor support to sustain treatment availability and resistance containment. The evaluations concluded that while the project made significant strides, it must address sustainability and diagnostic testing to ensure long-term success in malaria treatment and resistance management.

title: Independent evaluation of the International Household Survey Network (IHSN) and Accelerated Data Program (ADP)
file_title: Evaluation of the International Household Survey Network and Accelerated Data Programme
description: This document describes an evaluation of the International Household Survey Network (IHSN) and the Accelerated Data Programme (ADP), which aim to enhance statistical capacity and improve survey practices in developing countries. Conducted by Oxford Policy Management, the evaluation used document reviews, stakeholder interviews, country case studies, and eSurveys to assess the programs' relevance, impact, effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability. The IHSN/ADP were found to be successful in archiving surveys and increasing access to microdata, but faced challenges in coordination, collaboration, and demonstrating increased data usage. Recommendations include reaffirming partnerships, promoting microdata awareness, and developing strategic engagement with partner countries. The evaluation also suggests integrating the programs with broader development agendas and establishing a secretariat within a global institution. The estimated cost for the next five years is $22 million, with funding proposed from a multi-donor trust fund. Despite some concerns about funding processes and the need for a strategic focus, the programs are seen as relevant and effective, with a call for continued support and emphasis on developing future work plans and milestones.

title: Integrated Evaluation Report of the WiNN Programme
file_title: Management response: Working to Improve Nutrition in Northern Nigeria
description: The Integrated Evaluation Report of the WINNN Programme critically assessed a five-year initiative aimed at improving maternal and child nutrition in northern Nigeria. The programme's goals were to reduce malnutrition through various interventions, including community management of acute malnutrition and infant and young child feeding practices. The evaluation employed a diverse methodological approach, encompassing operations research, impact evaluation, economic evaluation, and gender analysis. Results showed some improvements in health service utilization but low intervention coverage and no significant enhancement in child nutrition status. The programme was sensitive to gender and aimed to reach marginalized groups, though with varying success. It increased political commitment and government capacity for nutrition work, despite systemic challenges. The report highlighted the cost-effectiveness of certain interventions but also pointed out financial concerns, such as the high cost of therapeutic foods. Recommendations for future programs included the need for better coverage data, increased public financing, and investment in multi-sectoral interventions, along with the establishment of a National Council on Nutrition. The evaluation underscored the importance of sustainability and scaling up services to effectively combat malnutrition.

title: Interim Evaluation of Taking Action: The UK Government's Strategy for Tackling HIV and AIDS in the Developing World
file_title: Annex 1 - List of people interviewed or consulted
description: This document describes an evaluation of the UK government's "Taking Action" strategy, aimed at addressing HIV and AIDS in developing countries. The strategy focuses on increasing financial support, which reached £385 million in 2005/6, advocating for more funding, harmonizing efforts, and supporting vulnerable groups. The evaluation, conducted by Social & Scientific Systems, Inc., used country case studies and working papers to assess the effectiveness of UK spending, decision-making, and the focus on key populations. While the UK is on track with its commitments, challenges such as a global funding gap, tracking allocations, and the need for coherent policies persist. Recommendations include ensuring access to services, supporting harm reduction, and enhancing monitoring and evaluation. The evaluation also reviews the integration of HIV and AIDS policies with other development issues, revealing successes like the influence on China's political leadership and the expansion of antiretroviral therapy, but also concerns about the continuity of support and the need for a systematic cross-government approach.

description: This document describes an evaluation of the KNOWFOR program, a collaborative initiative aimed at enhancing the use of forest-related knowledge in policy and practice for sustainable development. The program, involving partnerships with organizations like Clear Horizon, DFID, CIFOR, IUCN, and the World Bank's PROFOR, was assessed over a five-year period using a partner-led approach with external quality assurance. The evaluation employed various methodologies, including deep-dive case studies, economic analysis, and value for money analysis, to measure the program's effectiveness, influence on partners' core business, and financial efficiency. Results indicated that KNOWFOR achieved most of its performance targets, significantly influenced partners' approaches to Design, Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (DMEL), and contributed to gender mainstreaming in forestry and land use policy. Despite some challenges in collaboration and data quality, the program was considered to provide good value for money and to have laid a foundation for future initiatives. Recommendations were made to refine the Theory of Change, improve gender-responsive programming, and enhance DMEL systems, with an emphasis on sharing the methodology and findings to benefit similar programs.

description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of General Budget Support (GBS) and Programmatic General Budget Support (PGBS) in Burkina Faso from 1994 to 2004, assessing their effectiveness in poverty reduction, growth, and public financial management. The evaluation, conducted by various stakeholders including the International Development Department at the University of Birmingham, utilized the Enhanced Evaluation Framework and other methodological approaches such as data analysis, literature review, and causal chain analysis. The findings reveal that GBS and PGBS have positively influenced poverty reduction, public financial management, and aid effectiveness, particularly in the education and health sectors, and have improved donor coordination and alignment with national priorities. However, challenges such as weak government capacity, transparency issues, aid dependency, and the need for improved monitoring and accountability were identified. The evaluations emphasize the importance of government ownership, capacity building, and alignment with government policies for the success of GBS and PGBS, while also highlighting the moderate impact on governance and the sustainability of reforms. Recommendations include strengthening national stakeholder engagement, supporting government reforms, and enhancing coordination of capacity development initiatives to ensure more effective and sustainable outcomes.

title: Kenya Hunger Safety Net Programme Monitoring and Evaluation Component
file_title: Evaluation of the Kenya Hunger Safety Net Programme 2009 to 2012
description: This document describes a summary of the evaluation of the Hunger Safety Net Programme (HSNP) in northern Kenya from 2009 to 2012, aimed at reducing poverty and improving food security through unconditional cash transfers. The evaluation, conducted by Oxford Policy Management, utilized a randomized controlled trial and qualitative research to assess the program's impact. Results showed that the HSNP effectively reduced extreme poverty, increased consumption expenditure, and improved food security for smaller and poorer households. However, it did not significantly improve dietary diversity, child nutrition, or health status, though it did aid in coping with health shocks and retaining livestock. The program also positively affected school performance but not attendance or educational expenditure. It did not cause inflation, disrupt local markets, or create dependency, and it may have had positive local economic effects. The evaluation recommended targeting the poorest households and ensuring full entitlements to maximize impact, along with complementary interventions and further research on the program's various aspects.

title: Livelihoods and Food Security Trust Fund - Delta 1 Evaluation
file_title: Evaluation of livelihoods and food security trust fund
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Livelihood and Food Security Trust Fund (LIFT) program's interventions in Myanmar's Ayeyarwady Delta region post-Cyclone Nargis. The program's goal was to aid rice farmers and vulnerable populations by enhancing their income and food security through various means such as agricultural inputs, training, and resources. The evaluation employed focus groups, interviews, and surveys to measure the effectiveness and sustainability of the interventions, which included livestock distribution, agricultural equipment, and training programs. Results showed that while some interventions like buffalo distribution and seed banks were effective, others faced challenges due to local conditions and systemic risks. Training, particularly through Farmer Field Schools, was successful in disseminating knowledge and improving practices. However, issues with targeting, procurement, and the sustainability of cash-for-work programs were noted. The evaluation concluded that while the program positively impacted income and food security, improvements are needed to achieve pre-disaster levels and ensure long-term sustainability.

description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Chars Livelihood Programme (CLP-2) in Bangladesh, which aims to alleviate poverty and improve livelihoods on remote riverine islands. The program, supported by international funding, focuses on economic development, sustainability, and women's empowerment. A mixed-methods approach, including quantitative and qualitative research, was used to assess the program's impact on economic wellbeing, savings, assets, and empowerment. The findings reveal positive outcomes, with many households meeting graduation criteria and showing economic improvements. However, the report suggests that gains are not consistently rising and recommends future efforts to enhance productivity, market development, and resilience. The evaluation also examines the program's cost-effectiveness and sustainability, noting that while CLP-2 has reduced poverty and introduced sustainable practices, ongoing monitoring is necessary to ensure long-term success. Key challenges such as environmental shocks and social barriers are acknowledged, and strategies for addressing these issues are proposed.

Evaluations employed diverse methodologies, including desk research, interviews, focus groups, surveys, and numerical scoring tools, to assess the program's relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, sustainability, and value for money. description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the EU-Africa Infrastructure Trust Fund (ITF), which aims to enhance infrastructure development in Africa through investment in energy, transport, ICT, and water projects. The evaluation, conducted by various entities including Ernst & Young, utilized interviews, field visits, comparative analysis, and reviews of ITF documents and stakeholder feedback. The ITF has been successful in leveraging finance with a significant leverage ratio and has been crucial in advancing projects, particularly in meeting financial requirements and attracting additional funding. However, challenges such as slow disbursement rates, unclear objectives, over-subsidization risks, and governance issues were identified. Recommendations for improvement include refining objectives and leverage calculations, improving coordination among financiers, encouraging private sector participation, and enhancing monitoring and evaluation processes. The evaluation's findings are intended to inform future strategies and contribute to the final assessment of the ITF's impact and sustainability in infrastructure development across Africa.

description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of Zambia's Child Grant Program (CGP), which offers unconditional monthly cash transfers to households with young children to alleviate poverty and enhance food security. Results across different evaluations consistently show that the CGP has led to increased spending on essentials, improved food security, better child health outcomes, and economic benefits like higher household income and local economic stimulation. title: Nigeria Child Development Grant Programme Evaluation Quantitative Midline Report Volume I: Midline Findings
file_title: Child Development Grants Programme, Nigeria Volume 1
description: This document describes a comprehensive evaluation of the Child Development Grant Programme (CDGP) in northern Nigeria, which aims to alleviate poverty, hunger, and malnutrition through cash transfers and behavior change campaigns. The evaluation, employing a cluster randomized controlled trial and household surveys, reveals that the CDGP has positively impacted women's wellbeing, children's health, household food security, and knowledge and practices regarding nutrition and maternal health. Despite facing challenges such as imperfect coverage and potential biases, the program has shown improvements in women's work participation, earnings, household savings, and livestock ownership, as well as in maternal and child health knowledge and practices. However, the program's effects on men's work activities, income, and land cultivation were not significant. Additionally, while the CDGP has increased household expenditures and potentially influenced fertility rates, it has not significantly improved sanitation. The evaluation underscores the need for further research to understand the program's long-term effects and its influence on fertility, aiming to optimize its outcomes for the targeted communities.

description: This document summarizes an evaluation of DFID's support for health policy and systems guidance development from 1988 to 1998. The policy aimed to promote health sector reform and management, with a focus on developing countries in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa, and was geared towards achieving international targets such as halving extreme poverty by 2015. The evaluation, conducted by independent consultants, assessed the effectiveness of DFID's approach, which included supporting government policies, promoting reform, and developing national capacity for sector-level impact assessment. The findings indicated that success was more likely in countries with a clear commitment to reform and that a sector-wide approach to evaluation was necessary to address attribution issues. The evaluation also noted DFID's focus on the supply side of health services, the need for more attention to demand, and the limited impact of health systems research. It highlighted the importance of tailored interventions, inclusive and politically sensitive approaches, and the management of contractors. Lessons learned emphasized the need for comprehensive public sector reform, addressing gender inequalities through multi-donor initiatives, creating successful partnerships, and improving data collection and analysis. description: This document describes a summary of the final evaluation of the Nigeria Stability and Reconciliation Programme (NSRP), a five-year initiative funded by DFID aimed at managing conflict non-violently and reducing the impact of violence on vulnerable populations in Nigeria. The evaluation, conducted by various entities including WYG and the Centre for Research Documentation, used a mixed-method approach, such as case studies, surveys, and qualitative analysis, to assess the program's effectiveness in areas like strengthening peace architecture, involving marginalized communities, and influencing policy. The findings revealed a reduction in perceived violence and improvements in conflict management, but also highlighted challenges such as weak monitoring data, methodological issues, and concerns about the sustainability and inclusivity of the program's efforts. The evaluation provided recommendations for future programs, emphasizing the need for robust monitoring systems, real-time learning, adaptation to context, capacity development, and sustained behavioral change. Despite some successes in influencing policy and practice, the evaluation noted limited evidence of lasting change and questioned the long-term impact of the NSRP, suggesting that future initiatives consider economic and contextual factors, and adopt a holistic strategy for peacebuilding.

title: PO6414: Independent Evaluation of Wealth Creation Development of Rural Markets in Zambia

description: This document describes a summary of independent evaluations of a program designed to alleviate rural poverty in Zambia by integrating smallholder farmers into improved agricultural markets. The program, supported by DFID and Sweden, employed the Making Markets Work for the Poor (M4P) approach with the goal of sustainable market transformations. Evaluations utilized a variety of methods, including theory-based approaches, questionnaires, interviews, and focus groups, to assess the program's relevance, efficiency, effectiveness, impact, and sustainability. Results showed moderate impact with varying effectiveness across interventions, highlighting the importance of private sector investment and collaboration. Challenges included limited generalizability, lack of counterfactuals, and timing issues. Recommendations for future initiatives emphasized the need for comprehensive data collection, gender-targeted strategies, and flexibility in implementation. Overall, the program was moderately effective in creating systemic market changes, but further investment and time may be required to fully realize its potential.
